summary:
Space Watch is a web tool that lets anyone enter the coordinates of a patch of sky and watch SPHEREx infrared observations of it play back as a flipbook. Users can choose the field of view and detector, and share any position through the URL. Because every frame is aligned to the same grid, objects that move against the fixed background, such as nearby stars and brown dwarfs, jump out when the images are blinked. Difference and stack modes reveal moving and faint sources, and a spectrum plot shows how a target’s brightness changes across SPHEREx’s wavelengths.

SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months, producing far more data than astronomers can inspect alone. Most known brown dwarfs and comets were found by volunteers comparing images, but SPHEREx data is hard to use without programming skills. Space Watch removes that barrier. Its report feature lets users flag anything that moves or changes so others can check it.
details:
What it does

Users pick a challenge target or enter a Right Ascension and Declination, choose a field of view, and select one of SPHEREx’s six detectors or all six. Space Watch then plays every SPHEREx frame of that position in date order like a flipbook, with a frame slider, a speed slider and a pause button. The view is written into the URL (?ra=...&dec=...), so any position can be shared as a link or embedded in another website.

We built each tool to make changes easier to see.

Blink flips between selected frames, so anything that moved jumps while the stars stay still. Pluto was found the same way.
Difference subtracts an earlier frame from a later one. Unchanged sky turns grey, sources that got brighter show as white, and sources that faded or moved away show as black.
Stack averages frames to cut noise, which reveals sources too faint to see in a single frame.
Visits merges each of SPHEREx’s six-monthly passes into one cleaner image. Comparing visits months apart is where nearby stars and brown dwarfs show their motion.
Spectrum plots the target’s brightness at each wavelength from the raw data, which helps users work out what kind of object they are looking at. Clicking a point jumps to that frame.
On the test targets, an arrow shows the expected direction of motion, so users can check the tool against known stars.
Pressing Report or the space bar saves a note about the current frame and position for later review, and a separate Reports page lists every saved report. Reporting is how users contribute to research. Anyone who notices an object moving or changing can flag it, with the exact position and frame attached, so it can be followed up.

Benefits and intended impact

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared bands, which is far more data than astronomers can inspect alone. Using that data normally takes programming skills and specialist file formats. With Space Watch, anyone with a browser can explore real NASA observations and flag what they find.

Volunteers comparing sky images have already found most known brown dwarfs through projects like Backyard Worlds. We want Space Watch to bring that kind of public discovery to SPHEREx. Shareable URLs let anyone pass a find to someone else to verify. Reports are currently stored in the user’s own browser, and a shared public list is our next step.

The report feature is the heart of that goal. Space Watch is designed so that reports are sent to a separate server, where professional astronomers can review them and investigate the promising ones with follow-up observations. A member of the public with no training can notice a faint dot that moved, report it in one key press, and start a chain that ends with a confirmed new brown dwarf, comet or asteroid. In this first version reports are saved in the browser and read back on the Reports page, and connecting them to the review server is our next step.

How it works

Space Watch has a Python backend that does the astronomy and a single HTML page that does the viewing. The two only talk over HTTP, sharing a small JSON contract and a folder of PNG files.

For the challenge targets, the backend takes catalogue positions and proper motions and uses Astropy to carry each target forward to the middle of the SPHEREx coverage window, so the tool points at where the object actually is. For any position, the backend queries NASA’s IRSA archive for every SPHEREx exposure covering it, tags each with its detector and date, and sorts them in time order. Each exposure then goes through these steps to become a frame.

Only a small cutout around the target is downloaded, with a little padding.
The wavelength at the target’s pixel is read from the file header, since every pixel of a SPHEREx image sees a different wavelength.
The cutout is reprojected onto one shared north-up grid at 6.15 arcseconds per pixel. After this, the same pixel in every frame is the same patch of sky, so anything that appears to move really did.
Frames more than 15% invalid are dropped, and smaller holes from saturated stars are filled from neighbouring pixels.
A z-scale or arcsinh stretch is applied, chosen per target, and the frame is saved as a PNG, with a JSON file listing its date, detector, wavelength and archive URL.

The FastAPI server caches every build permanently, in a folder named after the coordinates and field of view. First builds run in a background thread with a progress bar and a quick 12-frame preview spread across the year, and repeat requests load instantly. A lock stops two identical requests from downloading the same data twice.

The frontend uses no libraries. When the user presses Go, it writes the query into the address bar and polls the backend every two seconds until the frames are ready. Choosing all detectors runs six of these at once and merges the results into one time-ordered list. It reads pixel values from a canvas to compute Difference, Stack and Visits in the browser. Visits splits the frames wherever SPHEREx was away for more than thirty days and averages each group. The spectrum uses aperture photometry on the raw data, summing the light around the target and subtracting the surrounding background, with results in millijanskys. The plot is drawn by the page itself as SVG.

How it’s creative

Most sky viewers show one image at a time. Space Watch lets users experiment with time and wavelength by blinking, subtracting and averaging any frames they choose, grouping them into visits, and jumping from any spectrum point back to its frame. The analysis runs in the browser, so results appear straight away.

The most creative part of Space Watch is that it doesn’t stop at showing the data. Other viewers end when the user closes the tab. Space Watch gives every user a way to act on what they see, by reporting any movement they notice. The design is for those reports to be passed to a separate server, reviewed by professionals and investigated further. That turns a viewing tool into a discovery pipeline, with the public doing the searching that no research team has the hours for, and astronomers spending their time only on the candidates worth checking. Blink, Difference, Stack and the spectrum all feed into this. They exist so that an ordinary person can make a report worth a professional’s attention.

Factors we considered

IRSA is slow and sometimes unavailable, so we pre-cached the five challenge targets and added automatic retries, progress reporting and previews.
Bright stars saturate the detectors and leave empty pixels, so we drop the worst frames and repair the rest.
Barnard’s Star has moved several arcminutes from its catalogue position, so we use SIMBAD proper motions and Astropy to calculate where each target was when SPHEREx observed it.
Browsers block reading pixels from images served by another server, so we serve frames with a cross-origin header that the analysis modes depend on.
Reports had to be effortless, so making one takes a single key press. We kept this first version simple by saving them in the browser, with the review server planned next.

Tools used

Python, FastAPI and Uvicorn for the backend. Astropy, astroquery and reproject for the astronomy. NumPy, SciPy and Pillow for image processing. HTML, CSS and JavaScript (Canvas and SVG) for the frontend. NASA’s IRSA archive for SPHEREx data. SIMBAD for positions and proper motions. Git and GitHub for teamwork.
